3. Results 3.1. Study selection and characteristics The systematic literature search identified 1199 records. After removal of duplicates, 871 unique records remained. Title and abstract screening yielded 23 articles for full-text assessment, of which 3 RCTs met the inclusion criteria [1] , [12] , [22] ( Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA 2020 Flow Diagram of Study Selection. Fig. 1 A total of 1156 patients were included across 3 RCTs. Of these, 579 patients (50.1%) underwent TAVI with preceding PCI, whereas 577 patients (49.9%) with significant CAD underwent TAVI only. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1 , Table 2 , and S4. The pooled cohort was elderly (median age 81–84 years) and predominantly male (64%). Most patients (90%) underwent transfemoral TAVI, with balloon-expandable device use ranging from 40% to 93% across trials. Surgical risk varied substantially between trials: the ACTIVATION trial enrolled a higher-risk cohort (median EuroSCORE 11.3–13.9%), whereas NOTION-3 and PRO-TAVI enrolled low-to-intermediate risk patients (median STS-PROM 3.0–3.1%) [1] , [12] . CAD complexity was low overall, with a median SYNTAX score of 9–10 in NOTION-3 and PRO-TAVI; however, SYNTAX scores were not reported in the ACTIVATION trial [22] . Cardiovascular risk factors were highly prevalent, including hypertension (74%), atrial fibrillation (34%), and diabetes mellitus (28%). Risk of Bias assessment All three trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool [1] , [12] , [22] . Although the trials were open-label, independent clinical events committees blinded to treatment allocation adjudicated all hard endpoints, which minimize detection bias (Fig. S1). 3.3. Primary efficacy endpoint: spontaneous MI Across the three included trials, spontaneous MI occurred in 29 of 579 patients (5.0%) with routine PCI versus 36 of 577 patients (6.2%) with deferred PCI. Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis comparing routine versus deferred PCI demonstrated a posterior median RR of 0.84 (95% CrI: 0.43–1.73), with a 70.2% posterior probability of any reduction (RR < 1.0) and a 43.2% probability of a clinically meaningful reduction (RR < 0.8). The 95% prediction interval crossed the null (0.29–2.72), and heterogeneity was low (τ = 0.28, 95% CrI: 0.00–0.81; I 2 = 26.3%). Sensitivity analyses using alternative priors produced consistent estimates (RR: 0.84–0.86; posterior probability of any reduction: 65.9%–70.2%), supporting the robustness of the primary findings. In the frequentist random-effects analysis, there was no statistically significant difference between routine and deferred PCI either with or without 95% CI correction (random-effects: RR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.49–1.31; p = 0.38; I 2 = 0.0%; random-effects with HKSJ correction: RR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.27–2.36; p = 0.48; Fig. 3 ). The overall grade of evidence is moderate, downgraded for imprecision attributable to wide intervals (Table S5). 3.3.2. Primary safety endpoint: major bleeding Major bleeding occurred in 91 of 579 patients (15.7%) assigned to routine PCI versus 57 of 577 patients (9.9%) assigned to deferred PCI. Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis yielded a posterior median RR of 1.56 (95% CrI: 0.91–2.71), with a 95.6% posterior probability of any increased risk (RR > 1.0) and an 83.2% probability of a clinically meaningful increase (RR > 1.25). The 95% prediction interval crossed the null (0.58–4.27), and heterogeneity was moderate (τ = 0.26, 95% CrI: 0.00–0.76; I 2 = 47.8%). Sensitivity analyses employing alternative priors produced consistent estimates (RR: 1.56 across all models; posterior probability of increased risk: 92.3%–95.6%), affirming the robustness of the primary findings. In the frequentist random-effects model, routine PCI was associated with a significantly higher risk of major bleeding relative to deferred PCI (RR 1.57, 95% CI: 1.07–2.32; p = 0.02), with low-to-moderate between-study heterogeneity (I 2 = 37.9%). However, after HKSJ correction, the 95% CI widened considerably and was no longer statistically significant (1.57, 95% CI: 0.65–3.81; p = 0.16; Fig. 4 ). The overall grade of evidence is moderate, downgraded for imprecision attributable to wide intervals (Table S5). 3.4. Secondary endpoints Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis demonstrated that routine PCI compared with deferred PCI yielded a median RR of 0.91 (95% CrI: 0.60–1.43) for all-cause mortality, with a 69.6% posterior probability of benefit [PPB] (RR < 1.0). Corresponding estimates for cardiovascular death, any MI, AKI, and stroke were 0.74 (95% CrI: 0.43–1.29; PPB: 87.8%), 0.83 (95% CrI: 0.43–1.75; PPB: 72.2%), 1.02 (95% CrI: 0.41–2.91; PPB: 48.5%), and 0.71 (95% CrI: 0.41–1.25; PPB: 90.0%), respectively. Routine PCI was associated with a reduced risk of any revascularization (RR 0.29, 95% CrI: 0.12–0.75; PPB: 99.0%) and urgent revascularization (RR 0.37, 95% CrI: 0.15–0.91; PPB: 98.1%). Conversely, bleeding risks were elevated with routine PCI: any bleeding (RR 1.76, 95% CrI: 1.06–2.88; posterior probability of harm [PPH]: 98.1%), life-threatening or disabling bleeding (RR 1.74, 95% CrI: 1.00–3.07; PPH: 97.4%), and minor bleeding (RR 1.96, 95% CrI: 1.09–3.48; PPH: 98.3%) (Figs. S2–S21). Sensitivity analyses using alternative priors (half-normal and half-Cauchy; scales 0.5 and 1.0) confirmed robustness across all secondary endpoints. Effect estimates, posterior probabilities, and heterogeneity estimates remained generally stable (Figs. S22–S31). Frequentist random-effects models yielded consistent results with Bayesian analyses ( Fig. 2 ). There was no statistically significant difference between routine and deferred PCI for all-cause mortality ( p = 0.40), cardiovascular mortality ( p = 0.12), MI ( p = 0.64), stroke ( p = 0.07), or AKI ( p = 0.76). However, routine PCI was associated with a statistically significant reduction in any revascularization ( p = 0.02) and urgent revascularization ( p = 0.02). Conversely, routine PCI was associated with a statistically significant increase in any bleeding ( p < 0.01), disabling or life-threatening bleeding ( p = 0.01), and minor bleeding ( p = 0.003). After HKSJ correction, the associations for revascularization and bleeding were no longer statistically significant (Figs. S32–S41). 3.5. Health-related and functional outcomes Two trials reported functional and anginal outcomes [1] , [12] . For functional status, the proportion of patients with NYHA class I-II was similar between groups (PCI 88.6% vs deferred 88.7%; RR 1.00, 95% CrI: 0.67–1.49), and NYHA class III-IV occurred in 11.4% of PCI patients vs 11.3% of deferred patients (RR 1.00, 95% CrI: 0.52–1.97). Frequentist analyses demonstrated no statistically significant differences ( p = 0.94 and p = 0.99, respectively). For anginal symptoms, the proportion of patients with CCS class I-II was numerically lower with routine PCI (10.7% vs 12.8%; RR 0.42, 95% CrI: 0.07–2.41), and CCS class III occurred in 0.3% of PCI patients vs 1.0% of deferred patients (RR 0.43, 95% CrI: 0.07–2.49), though credible intervals were wide. The proportion of patients with no angina (CCS class 0) was similar between groups (88.8% vs 86.2%; RR 1.03, 95% CrI: 0.69–1.54). Frequentist analyses were non-significant for all CCS endpoints. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness across all Bayesian models (Figs. S42–S56). 3.6. Major adverse cardiovascular events Under Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis, the median RR for MACE with routine PCI versus deferred PCI was 0.81 (95% CrI: 0.55–1.23), with an 88.6% PPB (RR < 1.0) and a 46.6% probability of a clinically meaningful reduction (RR < 0.8). The 95% prediction interval crossed the null (0.40–1.73). The frequentist pooled analysis yielded an RR of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.65–0.98; p = 0.03; I 2 = 0.0%); however, after HKSJ correction, the estimate was rendered non-significant ( p = 0.16). In sensitivity analyses, the estimate was attenuated: exclusion of NOTION-3 resulted in an RR of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.63–1.18; p = 0.36; I 2 = 0.0%), with corresponding Bayesian estimates of 0.88 (95% CrI: 0.47–1.68; PPB: 70.4%). Restriction to one-year landmark data to align follow-up durations across trials yielded an HR of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.67–1.18; p = 0.41; I 2 = 10.8%). Bayesian sensitivity analyses using alternative priors confirmed robustness ( Figs. 5 and S57). 3.7. Trial sequential analysis In the TSA, the cumulative Z -curve did not meet the required information size for the primary endpoints, any revascularization, or all-cause death. In contrast, the analysis was conclusive for any bleeding and for life-threatening or disabling bleeding, or for urgent revascularization, having surpassed the trial sequential monitoring boundaries, which suggests the current evidence is robust against type I and type II errors (Figs. S58–S64).
